q: What block height is needed for cervical cerclage under spinal anaesthesia?
why: A block to around T10 with sacral cover is enough; hyperbaric bupivacaine with a low-dose opioid.

q: From what gestation is an RSI used if GA is needed for cerclage?
why: Aspiration risk rises from the second trimester; RSI is used from around 18 weeks, with antacid prophylaxis.

q: In a twin pregnancy, how does spinal spread compare with a singleton pregnancy?
o: Around 2 dermatomes higher for the same dose
why: Twin pregnancy exaggerates singleton changes: higher spread, faster desaturation, more aortocaval compression and about double the blood loss.

q: After an accidental dural puncture during epidural siting, what proportion go on to develop PDPH?
why: Accidental dural puncture with a Tuohy needle occurs in about 1 in 100; 50–80% of those develop PDPH. After a spinal, PDPH is about 1 in 300.

q: What is the typical onset and positional nature of post-dural puncture headache?
o: 24–72 hours after puncture, worse sitting or standing and better lying flat
why: PDPH starts 24–72 hours after puncture, is fronto-occipital and postural; CN VI palsy and tinnitus can occur.

q: How much blood is typically injected for an epidural blood patch?
o: 20–30 ml, stopping if back or leg pain develops
why: Aim for about 20 ml (up to 30 ml), injected slowly; initial cure rate is 60–90%, better if done after 48 hours, and about 17% need a second patch.

q: A woman has a foot drop and numbness over the first web space after a long delivery in lithotomy. Which nerve is injured?
why: Common peroneal compression at the fibular head by lithotomy stirrups causes foot drop with numbness over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot (the first web space is its deep peroneal branch).

q: After labour epidural, a woman has back pain and a dense motor block that is not wearing off. What is the priority?
o: Urgent MRI and neurosurgical referral for epidural haematoma
why: Decompression within 6–12 hours of onset gives the best chance of recovery.

q: By how much is MAC reduced in pregnancy?
why: MAC falls by about 28% (from the first trimester); spinal doses are reduced by around 25% due to reduced CSF volume.

q: From what gestation does aortocaval compression become clinically important?
why: From about 20 weeks; neuraxial anaesthesia blunts the compensatory sympathetic response.
